extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo two-part test), including considerations such as improvements to technology, particular machines, particular transformations, and whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (primary framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: All claims must be evaluated for eligibility using the two-part test from Alice/Mayo: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) (Step 2A Prong One/Prong Two), and (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites significantly more than the exception (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) is a useful investigative clue but is not a stand-alone test; a claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test, and a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. See Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings, and other cited cases for application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to existing technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim demonstrates an improvement in an existing technological process or technology (as opposed to merely improving an abstract idea or business practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement is relevant across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). The improvement must be to technology/computers themselves (e.g., improving how a computer performs a task), not merely an improvement in an abstract concept. Examples of sufficient improvements include particular computerized methods that solve technical problems (McRO, Diamond v. Diehr, Rapid Litig. Mgmt.), new or improved servers/telephone systems, improved data compression methods, specific GUIs improving transaction accuracy, and improved processes for preserving biological material. Non-examples include applying a commonplace business method on a general purpose computer, using standard lab techniques, or merely gathering/analyzing information using conventional techniques (see cited case law). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail of computer involvement / specific recitation of how computer aids method
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that a computer's involvement improves technology, claims must recite details about how the computer aids the method, the extent of that aid, or the significance of the computer to performing the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding generic computer components or instructions to perform the method on generic machinery is not sufficient. If an applicant adds a 'generic computer' or claims it is 'specially programmed,' the examiner should assess whether those added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more than the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) and cases such as Ultramercial, TLI Communications, and Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the judicial exception is applied with, or by use of, a particular machine; the machine-or-transformation test is an important clue but not determinative by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims still must be analyzed under Alice/Mayo. If a machine is recited, consider whether that machine (or its recited elements) provides 'significantly more' than the exception. The M-or-T test can indicate patentability when a particular machine is recited, but satisfying M-or-T alone does not guarantee eligibility (see Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings). Examiners should also consider other Step 2B factors (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use/technological environment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine/apparatus elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which the machine or apparatus elements in the claim can be specifically identified (particular) versus being generic or broadly recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that recites a particular, specifically identified machine or concrete structural details is more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application (examples: Mackay Radio antenna claims; Eibel Process with Fourdrinier machine). A general-purpose computer that applies a judicial exception by conventional computer functions does not qualify as a 'particular machine.' Mere recitation of concrete/tangible components is not necessarily an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine/apparatus implements the steps of the method (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the machine plays an integral role in performing the claimed method steps (i.e., whether the machine implements the steps rather than merely serving as an object on which the method operates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use that enables the claimed method in a non-conventional way can integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. If the machine merely acts as an obvious mechanism or is only necessary for speed/automation, it likely does not add significantly more (see CyberSource; Versata discussion). Examiners should analyze whether the machine 'plays a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or mere field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the machine's involvement imposes meaningful limits on the claim or is merely nominal/insignificant (e.g., data-gathering steps or field-of-use limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally to the execution of the claimed method will not integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Data-gathering or stating the Internet as a data source without more are examples where machine recitation is insufficient. See Bilski, CyberSource, and MPEP §§ 2106.05(g),(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; such transformations are a clue to patentability for process claims that lack particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a particular article into a different state or thing can indicate the claim is significantly more than a judicial exception, but this is not a stand-alone test. 'Article' includes a physical object or substance that can be specifically identified; purely mental processes or mere data manipulation (basic mathematical constructs) are not considered eligible transformations. See Bilski, Gottschalk v. Benson, Tilghman example, and MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how specifically the transformation is described; more particular transformations are more likely to provide significantly more than an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing, smelting) show that definite chemical/physical transformations confine the monopoly and support eligibility. A highly particular transformation (with definite bounds/parameters) favors eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the recited article being transformed is specifically identified versus generically recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the transformation applies to a generically recited article or to 'any and all articles,' it is less likely to provide significantly more. Transformations that apply only to particular articles (or can be specifically identified) are more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature/type/extent of the transformation (change in state or function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the kind and extent of change effected by the transformation — whether the transformed article has a different state, function, or use versus e.g., mere relocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that produce a new/different function or use are more likely to provide significantly more; transformations that merely change location or do not materially alter function are less likely to do so. Example: transforming raw uncured rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr) provided significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible versus intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the transformation is of a physical/tangible object or an intangible concept (mental judgment, contractual obligation, data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a physical/tangible object or substance is more likely to provide significantly more (or integrate a judicial exception into a practical application) than transformation of an intangible concept. Purely mental processes are not considered eligible transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the transformation contributes meaningful limits to the claimed method or is merely an extra-solution activity/field-of-use that is nominal or insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that only amounts to a field-of-use limitation or nominal activity (e.g., administering a drug as merely a field-of-use in Mayo) will not provide significantly more. See Mayo and related discussion; see MPEP §§ 2106.05(g),(h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, determine whether any additional element(s) beyond the judicial exception are well-understood, routine, or conventional activity previously known in the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional elements are merely well-understood, routine, conventional activities recited at a high level of generality, they do not favor eligibility. Conversely, additional elements that are specific, unconventional, or confine the claim to a particular useful application of the exception can favor eligibility (example: DDR Holdings modified conventional internet hyperlinking behavior and was found eligible). Mayo provides an example where measuring metabolite levels by known techniques was held routine/conventional and insufficient. Examiners should consider overlap with the improvement consideration and other Step 2B factors (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known-in-art can still be unconventional (novelty separate from eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that is known in the art may nevertheless be unconventional or non-routine for purposes of eligibility; novelty/obviousness are distinct issues from Section 101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may improve conventional computer functionality and be eligible even if the improvement lacks novelty over the prior art. See Enfish (eligible despite anticipation in prior art) contrasted with related cases; assess whether the known element in context is unconventional or confining in a way that provides significantly more.
